planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Saperavi is unusually cold-tolerant for a Vitis vinifera variety and has proven reliable as far north as the Finger Lakes, but still needs a long warm season to fully ripen its thick-skinned, late-season clusters.

directions: Train young Saperavi vines onto a permanent trellis and prune to a cane or cordon system that keeps clusters well exposed to sun and air movement, which helps prevent rot given its moderately tight bunches. Saperavi's name derives from the Georgian word for 'dye' because it is a rare teinturier variety whose flesh, not just its skin, is deeply pigmented, yielding intensely dark, high-tannin, high-acid red wine traditionally fermented in buried clay qvevri vessels in eastern Georgia's Kakheti region. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once sugar and acid reach balance, as the variety ripens later than most reds but holds its acidity well even in warm years, making it useful in blends for structure and color. Beyond Georgia, Saperavi has become a benchmark cold-climate red for growers in New York, the Pacific Northwest, and parts of Eastern Europe.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — cold-climate red wine grape variety trials
Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes: A Complete Guide to 1,368 Vine Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container vines in early spring on a trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Rkatsiteli tolerates colder winters than most Vitis vinifera whites and has been grown commercially in the Finger Lakes for decades, though it still wants a reasonably long season to bring its high natural acidity into balance.

directions: Rkatsiteli is one of the world's oldest and most widely planted wine grapes by area, an ancient Kakhetian variety whose high yields, dependable vigor, and vigorous, somewhat sprawling canopy call for careful summer canopy management and shoot thinning to keep clusters from becoming overcrowded and prone to bunch rot. Its naturally high acidity and neutral-to-floral aromatics make it suitable for a remarkable range of finished styles, from crisp dry whites and sparkling base wine to the traditional amber qvevri wines of Georgia, where extended skin contact fermentation in buried clay vessels produces tannic, tea-colored wines. Harvest timing is a balancing act, since picking too early leaves wines sharply tart while late harvest softens the acid that defines the variety's character. Rkatsiteli's cold hardiness has also made it a mainstay test variety for cool-climate viticulture research in the northeastern United States and Eastern Europe.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — cold-climate white wine grape variety trials
Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes: A Complete Guide to 1,368 Vine Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container vines in early spring on a trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Mtsvane Kakhuri is somewhat less vigorous than Rkatsiteli and benefits from a sheltered, warm site since it is more susceptible to fungal pressure in humid conditions.

directions: Mtsvane Kakhuri (its name simply means 'green' in Georgian, referring to the grape's yellow-green skin) is a highly aromatic Kakhetian white variety traditionally interplanted and co-fermented with Rkatsiteli, where its floral, herbal aromatics soften Rkatsiteli's sharper acidity. Monitor clusters closely for powdery mildew and botrytis, since the variety's thinner skin and moderate bunch compactness make it more rot-prone than many Georgian natives, and keep the fruiting zone open with leaf pulling as clusters begin to color. Harvest when aromatics peak rather than waiting for maximum sugar, since Mtsvane's value in both dry white blends and traditional qvevri amber wine comes largely from its perfume. It remains a minor but prized variety almost exclusively grown within Georgia's wine regions.
sources: Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes: A Complete Guide to 1,368 Vine Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container vines in early spring on a trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Kisi was nearly lost to cultivation during the Soviet era in favor of higher-yielding varieties and is now being deliberately replanted, so stock is still mostly available through specialty Georgian and Eastern European nurseries.

directions: Kisi is a thick-skinned Kakhetian amber grape that was pushed to the edge of extinction during the Soviet consolidation of Georgian viticulture around a handful of commercial varieties, and has since been revived by natural-wine producers for its ability to withstand long skin-contact maceration in qvevri without turning harsh. Its heavy skin-to-juice ratio makes it well suited to extended amber-wine fermentation, developing notes of dried apricot, honey, and tannic grip that distinguish it from lighter-skinned whites. Thin canopies moderately to ensure adequate sun on developing clusters, since the thick skins that define the variety's character still need enough warmth to fully ripen. Harvest is typically later than other Kakhetian whites, once skins have developed full color and tannin.
sources: Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes: A Complete Guide to 1,368 Vine Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container vines in early spring on a trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Tsolikouri is adapted to the wetter, more humid climate of western Georgia's Imereti region, so good airflow through the canopy matters more for disease prevention than it does for drier-climate Kakhetian varieties.

directions: Tsolikouri is the principal white grape of Georgia's rainy western Imereti region, naturally high in acidity and productive enough to have historically served as the base for Soviet-era sparkling wine production in addition to still Imeretian whites. Because Imereti's humid climate puts more fungal pressure on vines than drier eastern regions, prioritize an open canopy, good row spacing, and timely leaf removal around fruit set to keep clusters dry. In traditional Imeretian winemaking, Tsolikouri is often fermented with a smaller proportion of skins and seeds than the amber wines of Kakheti, giving lighter, crisper results, though qvevri-fermented versions also exist. Harvest once acid levels begin to drop from their peak, since overripe fruit quickly loses the brightness that defines the variety.
sources: Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes: A Complete Guide to 1,368 Vine Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container vines in early spring on a trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Chinuri ripens late and keeps notably high acidity even at full maturity, so a long, consistently warm autumn improves results more than it does for earlier-ripening Georgian varieties.

directions: Chinuri, native to the Kartli region surrounding Georgia's old capital Mtskheta, is historically trained up living trees in the traditional maghlari system rather than on conventional trellising, though modern plantings typically use standard wire trellises for ease of management. The variety's defining trait is persistently high, almost tart acidity that holds up even at full ripeness, making it the traditional base for Georgia's naturally sparkling and semi-sparkling wines as well as skin-fermented amber styles. Because it ripens quite late, site selection for maximum autumn sun exposure matters more for Chinuri than for earlier Georgian varieties. Pick by taste and acid testing rather than a calendar date, since Chinuri's high-acid character can mask typical visual ripeness cues.
sources: Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes: A Complete Guide to 1,368 Vine Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container vines in early spring on a trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Khikhvi is prone to powdery mildew in damp conditions, so prioritize airflow and sun exposure through the fruiting zone over maximizing canopy density.

directions: Khikhvi is a highly aromatic Kakhetian amber variety known for pronounced floral and honeyed notes that intensify further when the grape is left on the vine into a light botrytis-affected state, historically used to make naturally sweet dessert wine as well as dry amber qvevri wine. Fruit set can be inconsistent in cool, wet springs, so a warm, sheltered planting site improves yield reliability. Keep an eye out for powdery mildew, to which the variety shows above-average susceptibility, and manage the canopy to maximize airflow around developing clusters. Harvest timing varies considerably by intended style, from relatively early picking for dry amber wine to extended hang time for dessert-style production.
sources: Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes: A Complete Guide to 1,368 Vine Varieties

planting.note: Transplant container-grown shrubs in early spring into humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil; this understory shrub of the Colchis forests of western Georgia tolerates more shade than most fruiting plants and appreciates shelter from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind.

directions: Jonjoli is the Georgian name for both the shrub Staphylea colchica and the unopened, still-green flower bud clusters harvested from it each spring before the small white-to-pink blossoms open. Pick the tight, unopened bud clusters in early-to-mid spring, then brine or vinegar-pickle them along with their stems for several weeks; the pickled buds develop a tangy, slightly nutty flavor reminiscent of capers and are traditionally served as a cold appetizer, often tossed with sliced onion and crushed walnuts, as part of a Georgian supra feast table. Established plants need only routine watering during dry spells and benefit from light thinning of old wood after flowering to encourage fresh bud-bearing shoots the following year. Because flower buds are the harvested part, avoid any pruning or fertilizing in late winter that would push growth past the tight-bud stage before harvest.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Staphylea colchica
